title: Kubernetes CI Needs a Mailbox Contract
summary:
Email verification is easy to treat as a tiny detail in a Kubernetes pipeline. A test creates a user, waits for a message, clicks a link, and reports green. The trouble starts when the mailbox is shared, the old message is still there, or the pod that created the test disappears before anyone can explain the failure.

I use a mailbox contract for these tests. It is a small set of rules that says who owns an inbox, how long it lives, what evidence belongs to the run, and when a missing message should block the deployment. The contract makes a burner email address behave more like an ephemeral infrastructure resource.

Why a mailbox needs a contract

Kubernetes gives every workload useful identity primitives: namespaces, labels, service accounts, and pod UIDs. A test mailbox needs the same kind of ownership. Without it, a CI job can find a valid-looking message that was created by a different run.

The contract should answer four questions:

  • Which pipeline run created this mailbox?
  • Which test or namespace is allowed to read it?
  • When does the mailbox expire?
  • What exact event proves that the email belongs to this run?

I also record a correlation ID in the application request and in the message lookup. A request ID is more reliable than a subject line, which may be translated or changed by a provider. The idea is similar to using session proof for email change APIs: the workflow should prove ownership, not just find a convenient message.

Define ownership and expiry

Give every test run a short identifier, for example ci-8f31a. Put it in the Kubernetes Job label, the test data, and the email event. The mailbox allocation record can then look like this:

{
  "run_id": "ci-8f31a",
  "namespace": "pull-requests",
  "owner": "github-actions",
  "created_at": "2026-10-22T05:20:00Z",
  "expires_at": "2026-10-22T05:35:00Z"
}

The expiry should be shorter than the normal retention period. If a test runs for ten minutes, a thirty-minute lease may be reasonable; a mailbox that hangs around for days is a source of stale evidence. Cleanup is sometimes forgotten, and that makes the next failure much harder to read.

For a workflow that needs a use and throw email during a non-production verification, a disposable service such as tempmailso.com can be one option. Keep the mailbox isolated from customer data and make the lease explicit. If the test needs to generate throwaway email addresses repeatedly, rate limits and provider errors should be handled as their own state, not silently retried forever.

Wire the contract into Kubernetes CI

The test worker can run as a short-lived Job. Pass only the run identifier and a reference to the mailbox lease; do not put inbox credentials in pod arguments or logs.

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  generateName: email-check-
  labels:
    app: email-check
    owner: github-actions
spec:
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 900
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: verifier
          image: registry.example.com/email-verifier:stable
          env:
            - name: CI_RUN_ID
              valueFrom:
                fieldRef:
                  fieldPath: metadata.uid

The pod UID is useful for tracing, but I still pass a CI run ID from the pipeline because it is easier to find in build logs. A small Docker image is enough; the important part is that the worker emits structured results such as matched, timeout, wrong_owner, or provider_error.

The pipeline can then collect a bounded result:

kubectl -n pull-requests wait --for=condition=complete \
  job/email-check --timeout=120s
kubectl -n pull-requests logs job/email-check --tail=100

Do not make kubectl logs the only record. Export the final status, run ID, message ID, and timestamps as CI artifacts before cleanup. This is where request IDs in signup checks become useful beyond application code: the same identifier ties the browser action, API request, email, and deployment record together.

Choose blocking and warning behavior

Not every email failure should stop an AWS deployment. I normally use three outcomes:

  1. Block: the email is part of the feature being released and the expected message is missing or belongs to another run.
  2. Warn: the application is healthy, but a non-critical notification provider timed out.
  3. Retry: the provider returned a known transient error, with a fixed retry count and deadline.

The check is simple, but it are easy to make the retry path unlimited. Put the deadline in the test output so an operator can tell whether the failure came from Kubernetes, the application, or the external mailbox service. A generic “email failed” message sends people to the wrong dashboard.

Keep evidence after the pod is gone

Short-lived jobs are good for isolation, but they remove local context quickly. Before deleting the namespace or Job, save a small receipt containing the deployment SHA, namespace, run ID, mailbox lease, correlation ID, result state, and message timestamp. Never store the full message when a header or message ID is enough.

I also check that a failed run cannot read a previous run's inbox. This negative test catches the bug better than another happy-path signup. In practice, teams often write temp mailid or tepm mail com in notes while searching for a service; those strings are not an ownership mechanism, so the test still needs a real lease and correlation check.

Final checklist

Before making the email check a deployment gate, verify:

  • every mailbox has a run owner and expiry time
  • the correlation ID is present in logs and lookup filters
  • stale messages are rejected
  • the Kubernetes Job has a bounded timeout
  • provider errors are separate from application failures
  • CI artifacts retain a minimal evidence receipt
  • cleanup runs even after a failed test
  • the blocking policy is documented for the team

This contract is small, but it removes a surprising amount of guesswork. The mailbox becomes a named dependency with a lifecycle, instead of a hidden shared state that occasionally makes CI green for the wrong reason.

title: The Hidden Engineering Behind Every “Remember This?” Moment
summary:
**The Hidden Engineering Behind Every “Remember This?” Moment
The product request sounds modest: show people a few meaningful photos, add a video recap, and give them a reason to return. The prototype looks convincing by Friday. Then an imported library overwhelms processing, a video stalls on mobile data, and a deleted photo reappears inside a cached collection. Suddenly, your memories feature involves queues, identity, media delivery, and incident response. For Android developers, CTOs, and founders evaluating a photo memories SDK for Android apps, the real decision is how much of that machinery to build, operate, and keep aligned with the product experience customers expect.

1. The Visible Problem: A Simple Feed Becomes a Distributed Feature

Users experience memories as a single interaction. They tap a story ring and expect relevant content to appear quickly. They do not distinguish between an upload service, a processing worker, a collection API, and a device cache. When any component fails, the entire feature feels unreliable.
Product managers encounter a different symptom: the scope keeps expanding. A carousel needs thumbnails and viewed states. A video feed needs playback controls, lifecycle handling, and recovery after interruptions. Personalization needs usable metadata, selection rules, and enough eligible material. Deletion introduces coordination across every representation of the original asset.
The first architectural mistake is treating these requirements as independent tickets. They form a connected data lifecycle. A collection generated successfully yesterday may be invalid today because its permissions changed. A responsive API can still deliver a poor experience when media takes several seconds to start. A beautiful interface cannot compensate for irrelevant selections.
Sparse libraries deserve particular attention. New users may have only a handful of uploads, while established accounts can contain years of duplicates, screenshots, and edited exports. Generating something for everyone is not necessarily a useful objective. Sometimes the correct result is an intentional empty state rather than a weak collection.
Android adds lifecycle complexity to this already distributed system. Playback must respond appropriately when an activity pauses, a screen rotates, or another application takes audio focus. Account switching must also prevent previous results from appearing during a fresh session. Comparable concerns exist on iOS, although the platform APIs and implementation details differ.
For engineering leaders, the useful starting point is a responsibility map. Identify who owns eligibility, processing, publication, authorization, playback, and support. That exercise exposes the difference between a working prototype and a feature that can survive growth without diverting the core application team into permanent media infrastructure maintenance. Fyrememories Blogs

2. The Architecture: From Uploaded Asset to Reliable Playback

Make processing recoverable before making it fast
A photo memories processing pipeline should begin with a durable asset identity. Associate the object with its account, record its version where available, and verify eligibility before analysis. Upload completion establishes that storage accepts a file; it does not establish that a memory is ready.
Use events to schedule background work rather than blocking the upload response on media analysis. Event consumers must respect their source’s delivery guarantees. Amazon S3 notifications, for example, can arrive more than once and do not guarantee event ordering. [1] Processing should therefore tolerate replay without publishing duplicate results.
An application-owned job might carry the following fields. This is an illustrative internal payload, not a FyreMemories endpoint or documented request schema:
{
"tenantId": "tenant_42",
"assetId": "asset_918",
"sourceVersion": "v3",
"processorVersion": "analysis_2",
"jobKey": "tenant_42:asset_918:v3:analysis_2"
}
Use the job key to identify repeated work, claim jobs atomically, and persist the outcome. Deduplication must extend to publication: a worker can crash after writing output but before acknowledging its event. Retrying should recover the existing result or replace it safely.
Historical imports need separate capacity planning. A large archive can consume workers intended for recent uploads. Bound concurrency, apply retry backoff, and monitor the oldest waiting job. Separate workload lanes where necessary, with explicit limits that protect interactive expectations while imports progress.
Give the pipeline a shared vocabulary for states such as pending, processing, ready, failed, and removed. A client should not have to infer readiness from missing fields. Include a collection revision in your own response model so consumers can recognize changes without confusing an updated result with a new memory.
Observability should follow the same boundaries. Propagate correlation identifiers between processing and publication, then link retrieval failures to the relevant collection. Avoid logging personal media, access tokens, or signed delivery URLs. Record enough structured context to distinguish unsupported inputs from temporary dependency failures. This makes debugging faster and reduces the temptation to reproduce every incident by manually opening customer content. It also gives support teams a concrete starting point during escalation.

Keep source access narrow and derived data traceable

Processing inside the customer’s cloud can preserve the existing storage arrangement and avoid copying originals into another provider’s storage. However, location alone does not establish a complete privacy boundary. Document where summaries, derived media, collection records, analytics, and delivery caches reside.
A read-only storage permission should grant only the source access the processor requires. Processing jobs may still create summaries or derived records elsewhere, so review their outputs and destinations separately. Keep permission management, runtime deployment, and operational logging visible to the responsible engineering team.
Preserve capture time separately from upload time. An old photograph imported today should not automatically become a recent event. Record metadata provenance and processing versions so future changes remain explainable. Link each generated collection to its source assets, enabling targeted invalidation when content becomes ineligible.
Deletion also creates a race: a worker may finish after the source has been removed. A tombstone or revision check can prevent stale work from publishing, provided that publication coordinates with the current eligibility state. The server must enforce authorization independently of any user identifier supplied by the client.

Separate metadata caching from media delivery

A fast feed usually combines several caches with different purposes. Collection metadata helps the interface render its structure. Thumbnails support browsing. Video data supports playback. Giving all three the same retention policy makes it harder to control disk use, freshness, and account isolation.
For metadata, consider a bounded freshness window with background revalidation where your access model allows it. Sensitive permission changes may require stricter invalidation. Use asset versions to distinguish updated media from older cached representations, and include account scope wherever cache entries could otherwise overlap.
Measure API response time separately from tap-to-first-frame latency. The latter includes media access, network transfer, player preparation, and decoding. Track cold and warm sessions independently; a warm-cache average can hide a poor first encounter.
Preloading can reduce visible waiting, but it shifts work earlier rather than eliminating it. Fetching the next likely video may be useful. Fetching several complete videos for someone who leaves immediately wastes transfer and storage. Adapt budgets to connectivity, user preferences, device constraints, and observed viewing behavior.
Adaptive bitrate streaming is a separate architectural choice. It requires multiple encoded renditions and a supported manifest format, such as HLS or DASH, so the player can select an appropriate stream. A single MP4 with next-item prefetch is not equivalent. Confirm the provider’s actual delivery formats before assuming adaptive streaming is included.
The SDK-versus-custom-UI decision follows the same principle. Standard components reduce presentation work; a headless integration preserves control but returns layout, accessibility, interaction, and lifecycle responsibilities to your team. Choose based on the experience you need to own, not simply the amount of code in the initial demonstration. Fyrememories Blogs

3. The Business Impact: Engineering Scope Becomes Operating Cost

The cost of memories infrastructure is rarely represented by one subscription line. It includes integration work, processing compute, source reads, media delivery, observability, support, and ongoing compatibility testing. An inexpensive component can become costly if it leaves the surrounding operating model undefined.
Consider an illustrative planning estimate, not a vendor quote or industry benchmark. If two engineers each spend 20 hours integrating playback and presentation, another engineer spends 24 hours connecting backend events, and validation requires 16 hours, the initial allocation is 80 engineering hours. It excludes design, production hardening, and future maintenance.
The purpose of that estimate is to make scope visible. Replace every assumption with your own backlog and staffing rates. Compare an SDK and an internal build against the same acceptance criteria, including account transitions, empty libraries, failures, and deletion. Comparing a vendor’s production integration with an internal prototype produces misleading economics.
Bandwidth creates another concrete trade-off. Suppose 100,000 monthly viewing sessions each download an unnecessary 8 MB through overly aggressive preloading. That amounts to roughly 800 GB of additional transfer in decimal units. Whether it becomes billable egress depends on the delivery path and commercial agreements, but the wasted bytes remain observable.
Set performance targets within a defined test environment. For example, a team could propose p95 tap-to-first-frame below 1.5 seconds on a specified device and network profile. This is an illustrative acceptance target, not a FyreMemories benchmark. Pair it with downloaded bytes per session and rebuffering measurements so faster startup does not conceal excessive resource consumption.
Retention needs similar discipline. Track how many eligible users see the entry point, open a collection, watch meaningfully, and return later. Completion rate can identify viewing behavior, but it cannot independently prove incremental retention. Users with richer libraries may already be more engaged before the feature appears.
A controlled rollout helps separate correlation from impact. Define the comparison group, observation window, and guardrails before launch. Include crash rates, startup performance, and support contacts alongside engagement. A feature that increases viewing while destabilizing the main application may deliver little overall value.
Maintenance is another recurring budget item. Android platform changes, dependency conflicts, decoder behavior, and authentication updates can require investigation long after the launch sprint. Establish who reproduces bugs, who supplies fixes, and how your team validates upgrades. A vendor relationship reduces uncertainty only when escalation paths and supported configurations are clear.
Time-to-market matters because delayed learning also has a cost. A suitable SDK can bring the first measurable release forward by reducing implementation scope. The strategic benefit is strongest when your team can spend that recovered time on differentiation, customer feedback, and product experiments instead of repeatedly maintaining generic playback infrastructure. Fyrememories Blogs

4. How FyreMemories Addresses This

FyreMemories combines a native Android memory experience with a processing platform. Its documented architecture keeps originals in the customer’s cloud, processes incoming uploads there, and passes summaries downstream for indexing and memory generation. Teams can retain their existing upload flow while evaluating a managed generation layer.
The source boundary is explicit: the processor requires read access to customer storage. Your deployment review should still establish runtime responsibilities, summary fields, retention, and deletion behavior. Keeping original files in place simplifies one part of integration; the complete operating agreement still deserves engineering scrutiny.
On Android, FyreMemories offers a story carousel, a full-screen feed, and a headless repository. These support different integration depths. Standard surfaces can reduce custom interface work, while repository access lets teams build a distinct presentation around the returned data.
**Initialize after authentication, then bind the experience
The public SDK documentation requires a signed-in Firebase user before initialization. Place initialization in your authenticated application flow, with a clear owner, rather than assuming a restored user is available during application startup. The following excerpt assumes dependency setup, imports, and the host authentication flow already exist: [2]
// Run after the host app confirms Firebase authentication.
if (FirebaseAuth.getInstance().currentUser != null) {
FyreMemories.init(context = applicationContext)
}
After initialization, an Activity containing the carousel view can bind it to the current user. The layout must already declare the view with the matching identifier; this excerpt shows the binding step rather than a complete Activity: [2]
val userId = FyreMemories.currentUserId()
if (userId != null) {
val carousel =
findViewById(R.id.memoriesCarousel)

carousel.bind(lifecycleOwner = this, userId = userId)

}
These small integration points should sit inside a larger lifecycle plan. Decide how the host screen handles unavailable content, where navigation opens the feed, and how authentication transitions stop old requests and presentation. Documented SDK methods reduce plumbing, but they do not replace application-level acceptance testing.
**Choose defaults deliberately and measure the result
FyreMemories documents separate thumbnail and video cache budgets, next-video prefetch controls, and per-user state. Its sign-out guidance includes a cleanup method. Review these controls against your expected session length, device storage constraints, and account-switching behavior before selecting production settings.
Built-in engagement analytics and integration hooks can reduce instrumentation work. They give product teams a starting point for observing viewing behavior, while engineering teams should connect those signals with application reliability and delivery measurements. Confirm event definitions before combining SDK analytics with your existing reporting.
For a photo memories SDK for Android apps, the practical evaluation is an integrated pilot. Use representative libraries, mixed media, historical imports, and unreliable networks. Verify how the feed behaves after permissions change, when no memories exist, and when a user leaves during preloading.
Make the pilot reviewable by recording the environment and expected outcome for each scenario. For a large import, capture queue age and time until the first usable collection. For interrupted viewing, record recovery behavior and repeated downloads. For account changes, verify that previous content disappears before the next user’s experience becomes available.
Also plan how you will reverse a rollout. Your application should be able to hide the entry point without affecting uploads or core navigation. Decide how a disabled feature handles pending requests and cached presentation. This limits the impact of an integration problem while your team investigates with the provider.
The public material currently centers on native Android integration. Teams planning iOS should confirm availability, feature parity, and delivery commitments directly rather than assuming a matching SDK. The architectural principles transfer across platforms, but implementation support is a separate procurement question.
FyreMemories is a fit to investigate when your team wants a managed memory layer and reusable presentation components while retaining its existing source storage. The buying decision should rest on measured integration effort, verified behavior, and an agreed division of responsibilities. Fyrememories Blogs

**5. Frequently Asked Questions

Should we build a photo memories feature ourselves or use an SDK?

Build internally when owning selection, processing, and playback behavior is central to your differentiation and you can fund their ongoing operation. Evaluate an SDK when reusable infrastructure can shorten delivery while preserving required controls; compare both options against the same workload and failure scenarios.

Does a memory SDK reduce cloud costs automatically?

No. Caching and bounded preloading can reduce repeated downloads, but processing, derived assets, and speculative transfer still consume resources. Measure the full delivery path and include your own cloud charges alongside provider fees before concluding that an integration lowers costs.
A convincing “Remember this?” moment is the visible result of reliable processing, useful selection, careful access control, and efficient playback. Your next step is to test those responsibilities together. Explore the FyreMemories SDK documentation and platform features, then run an Android integration pilot with your own assets, authentication flow, and measurable acceptance criteria.

A fast feed usually combines several caches with different purposes. Collection metadata helps the interface render its structure. Thumbnails support browsing. Video data supports playback. Giving all three the same retention policy makes it harder to control disk use, freshness, and account isolation.
For metadata, consider a bounded freshness window with background revalidation where your access model allows it. Sensitive permission changes may require stricter invalidation. Use asset versions to distinguish updated media from older cached representations, and include account scope wherever cache entries could otherwise overlap.
Measure API response time separately from tap-to-first-frame latency. The latter includes media access, network transfer, player preparation, and decoding. Track cold and warm sessions independently; a warm-cache average can hide a poor first encounter.
Preloading can reduce visible waiting, but it shifts work earlier rather than eliminating it. Fetching the next likely video may be useful. Fetching several complete videos for someone who leaves immediately wastes transfer and storage. Adapt budgets to connectivity, user preferences, device constraints, and observed viewing behavior.
Adaptive bitrate streaming is a separate architectural choice. It requires multiple encoded renditions and a supported manifest format, such as HLS or DASH, so the player can select an appropriate stream. A single MP4 with next-item prefetch is not equivalent. Confirm the provider’s actual delivery formats before assuming adaptive streaming is included.
The SDK-versus-custom-UI decision follows the same principle. Standard components reduce presentation work; a headless integration preserves control but returns layout, accessibility, interaction, and lifecycle responsibilities to your team. 3. The Business Impact: Engineering Scope Becomes Operating Cost

The cost of memories infrastructure is rarely represented by one subscription line. It includes integration work, processing compute, source reads, media delivery, observability, support, and ongoing compatibility testing. An inexpensive component can become costly if it leaves the surrounding operating model undefined.
Consider an illustrative planning estimate, not a vendor quote or industry benchmark. Bandwidth creates another concrete trade-off. Suppose 100,000 monthly viewing sessions each download an unnecessary 8 MB through overly aggressive preloading. That amounts to roughly 800 GB of additional transfer in decimal units. Whether it becomes billable egress depends on the delivery path and commercial agreements, but the wasted bytes remain observable.

Pair it with downloaded bytes per session and rebuffering measurements so faster startup does not conceal excessive resource consumption.
Retention needs similar discipline. Track how many eligible users see the entry point, open a collection, watch meaningfully, and return later. Completion rate can identify viewing behavior, but it cannot independently prove incremental retention. Users with richer libraries may already be more engaged before the feature appears.
A controlled rollout helps separate correlation from impact. Define the comparison group, observation window, and guardrails before launch. Establish who reproduces bugs, who supplies fixes, and how your team validates upgrades. A vendor relationship reduces uncertainty only when escalation paths and supported configurations are clear.

Keeping original files in place simplifies one part of integration; the complete operating agreement still deserves engineering scrutiny.
On Android, FyreMemories offers a story carousel, a full-screen feed, and a headless repository. These support different integration depths. Standard surfaces can reduce custom interface work, while repository access lets teams build a distinct presentation around the returned data.

FyreMemories.init(context = applicationContext)
}

if (userId != null) {
val carousel =
findViewById(R.id.memoriesCarousel)

carousel.bind(lifecycleOwner = this, userId = userId)

}

**5. Frequently Asked Questions

Should we build a photo memories feature ourselves or use an SDK?

Build internally when owning selection, processing, and playback behavior is central to your differentiation and you can fund their ongoing operation. Evaluate an SDK when reusable infrastructure can shorten delivery while preserving required controls; compare both options against the same workload and failure scenarios.

No. Caching and bounded preloading can reduce repeated downloads, but processing, derived assets, and speculative transfer still consume resources. Measure the full delivery path and include your own cloud charges alongside provider fees before concluding that an integration lowers costs.
A convincing “Remember this?” moment is the visible result of reliable processing, useful selection, careful access control, and efficient playback. title: Anyone can attack now, with AI — check your own site first
summary:
This is part 1 of the series "Protect Your Own Service Yourself — Self-Defense Security in the Age of AI." Do the checks you can yourself; when it's hard, EarthLink Network can run the assessment for you, and fix the gaps you can't fix on your own.

Series contents

  1. Anyone can attack now, with AI — check your own site first (this article)
  2. What attackers now hold: when AI runs the attack itself (coming soon)
  3. Before you start: test only what is yours, without breaking production (coming soon)
  4. Testing from the outside (1): setup and the first run (coming soon)
  5. Testing from the outside (2): attack tools and legitimate scanners find different things (coming soon)
  6. Checking the code you wrote: static analysis (coming soon)
  7. Checking the parts you depend on: libraries and packages (coming soon)
  8. Checking your infrastructure settings for gaps (coming soon)
  9. Collect every result in one place and decide what to fix first (coming soon)
  10. How to fix what you found: three ways (coming soon)
  11. When you cannot fix it yourself: a maintenance contract (coming soon)
  12. Keep checking automatically every day — from building to protecting (coming soon)

In the summer of 2025, a free attack tool called Villager went up on a public site where developers share code. You tell it "look into this site," and an AI decides on its own where to look, what to try, and what to do next. In about two months, before the press picked it up, it was downloaded roughly 10,000 times.

That is the starting point for this series. Attack tools like this are now free and available to anyone. The people who attack already have them and are already using them. So instead of finding out after a break-in, check your own service yourself first, find the weak spots, and fix them. That is the most reliable defense you have.

Security is no longer only a problem for companies big enough to be targeted. Even if nobody has heard of you, machines now try every site on the internet, one after another. This part explains why that matters now, and what the series will do.

All 12 parts of this series

Here is the plan, up front.

  1. Part 1 (this one): why do this now. The thinking behind it, and how the series runs.
  2. Part 2: what tools attackers hold today, and what it means for an AI to run an attack by itself. Not how to get them, but what such an opponent can do.
  3. Part 3: what to decide before you start testing. Test on a separate copy of your setup so you do not break the live service your customers use, and never look into anything that is not yours.
  4. Part 4: testing from the outside. Setup and the first run.
  5. Part 5: the results of testing from the outside. We compare what attack tools find with what legitimate security scanners find.
  6. Part 6: checking the code you wrote by reading it without running it (static analysis).
  7. Part 7: checking the parts you depend on (libraries and packages) for known weaknesses. This is where findings tend to pile up.
  8. Part 8: checking your server and cloud settings for gaps.
  9. Part 9: collecting the scattered results in one place and deciding what to fix first, including the risk from partners and parts you are connected to.
  10. Part 10: how to fix what you found. There are three ways.
  11. Part 11: when you cannot fix it yourself, the option of a maintenance contract.
  12. Part 12: keep the checks running automatically every day. From building things to protecting them.

The service we test is promptflow, a service our own company builds and runs.

October 2026: breach announcements kept coming

In October 2026, data breach announcements did not stop. In the US, the count of people affected by the 2025 breach at Oracle's health division (formerly Cerner) rose to about 20 million. Heart monitor maker iRhythm disclosed that data on about 8.2 million people had been stolen. In the UK, online retailer ASOS disclosed a leak of customer data, and Frontline Education, which makes software for schools, disclosed a leak of school staff data. In Japan, the parcel carrier Yamato Transport announced a leak of 5.31 million records of personal data, and one count found more than 40 breach announcements there in about a month.

Ransomware is an attack that locks or steals a company's data and demands payment to give it back. Worldwide, according to the security company Bitdefender, the criminals behind it named 790 organizations as victims in September alone, the month before, 30% more than in September a year earlier.

Numbers like these can feel like someone else's problem. What caught my attention was who the victims were: a parcel carrier, an online store, health care companies, school administration. Ordinary companies, with no special reason to be targeted.

The victims were not special companies

Reading the reports, I noticed something else. The way in was not special either. A partner's server. Setting mistakes in an API (the set entry point that other systems and apps use to request data from a service) or in an admin screen. An old bug in a piece of software. A password that someone reused and that leaked elsewhere. Put them side by side, and these are ordinary paths that many companies have right now.

Take the reused password. Some other service, nothing to do with you, leaks a list of email addresses and passwords. The attacker enters those pairs, one after another, into hundreds of unrelated sites. Wherever someone reused the password, the login goes through. Nobody broke into your site. A password that leaked from some other service, and that your user had reused, simply worked on it. A machine does this nonstop, not a person. So even if your own password handling is solid, someone can get in because of what happened on the user's side.

Attacks also work in a different order now. A human attacker chose a target first, with a motive, and spent time on one company. Automated attacks go through the whole internet mechanically, site after site, and pick up whatever happens to have a hole. Whether your service is famous or large does not matter. If it is public and has a hole, that is enough. So "nobody would bother with a small business like us" does not hold. You are not being targeted; everything is being checked at once.

Attacks no longer need special skills

This is the biggest change. Until recently, attacking took real skill: a person had to work out for themselves where to look and what to try next.

Think of a door lock. The common pin tumbler lock, where you insert a key and turn it, could be picked by a skilled person with thin metal picks, setting the pins one at a time by feel. Few people could do that, and that was part of the protection. Then came devices you simply hold against the lock: press a button, and the lock turns. No skill needed. That is why people moved to locks that are harder to copy and pick, such as dimple keys, with rows of small dents on the surface.

The same thing is happening in security right now.

AI now plans the steps of an attack

Since around the summer of 2025, tools that hand the planning of an attack to an AI have been given away for free.

Villager, from a Chinese company, is the example I opened with. Part 2 covers what it does in detail.

Villager is not the only one. Several tools like it, where AI runs the attack by itself, sit on public code-sharing sites and have been copied many times. How far have they spread? One has about 7,700 copies (forks, where someone copies the project to keep their own version), another about 4,700, another about 2,900. When one gets attention, hundreds of similar copies spread right away. That is how free software works. It is not something anyone can stop.

Some of these are legitimate tools built for defenders, presented as a way to "find and fix the weaknesses in your app." In this series we use both kinds on our own service, because you only learn where someone can really get in by checking the way attackers do it. Then we show how their findings differ.

My point here is not about good or bad. It is a fact: the skill barrier has dropped to almost zero. One short instruction, and anyone, in theory even a child, can move an attack forward. The time when skill itself was the protection is almost over.

Small companies are the least likely to have checked

Small companies are the most exposed to these automated attacks. Large companies have security staff who test their systems regularly, and budget for outside firms. Sole proprietors and companies of a few people have neither. So the businesses that have checked the least are probed by these automated scans just as often as everyone else. They have not checked, so they do not know they have weak spots, and they learn about it only after the leak.

This is why I care about tools that run with one click. If a tool does the planning, a small company without security staff can still run a check at least once. As long as checking takes expert knowledge, people stop at "I know it matters, but we can't." The same thing that lowered the barrier to attack has lowered the barrier to checking. Not all of this is bad news.

Hiding information only hurts the defenders

Whenever I write like this, I get the same pushback: "Don't name those tools. You're giving attackers a lead." I think that idea is backwards.

Attackers do not learn about tools from honest articles like this one. They got them elsewhere, long ago, and that is why they are attacking right now. The pile of breaches in October 2026 is the proof. Keeping quiet did not prevent any of them.

So who is hurt when information is hidden? Only the people with no other way to find it: the defenders. Attackers already know which tools are out there and what they can do; only the defenders do not. They do not even know where they are exposed. That is the most dangerous state to be in.

Defenders benefit from this being public. Once it is known which weakness a tool goes after, software makers can fix it quickly and users can review their settings. If it were hidden, nobody could fix anything, and attackers would quietly keep using it.

It was the same with locks. Keeping a lock's design secret does not help if the lock is weak. A strong lock is strong because it holds even when everyone knows how it works. Software security is the same: do not protect it by hiding, build it to hold up when it is known. That is why, in this series, I name the tools, say what they do, and show the results of checking our own service, without hiding any of it.

First, check your own service yourself

What to do is simple. Take the same tools attackers use, run them against your own service first, find the weak spots, and fix them. If a key that works on almost any lock is on sale, first see whether it works on your own door. If it does, switch to a stronger lock. That is all.

We limit the target to our own service, promptflow, for two reasons. Because it is ours, we decide how far to test, and we can make sure the test copy does not reach real users or outside services. And we are the ones best placed to fix its weak spots. Doing the whole loop of testing, finding, and fixing on something we own seemed the most honest and useful way to show it.

promptflow is a service we build and run for working with AI. Users log in, it holds data, and it connects to other systems through APIs. It has the same kinds of entry points used in the October 2026 breaches, which makes it a good subject. If we find a weak spot in ours, the same spot may be weak in yours. We show the steps exactly as we run them, so you can check the same things on your service.

"Is it safe?" is a call a person makes after testing

I believe that from now on, people's job is to make decisions: AI does the drafting, and people make the final call. "Is my service safe?" is exactly this kind of decision. And a decision needs facts from real testing. Saying "it's probably fine" without testing is not a decision. It is a hope.

Until recently, attackers had the advantage: their attacks were automated, while defenders checked by hand, one thing at a time. Now defenders can use the same automation. If attackers can try with one click, so can we. There is no reason not to use it.

What we will actually do in this series

From Part 4, we test promptflow for real. Here is the approach, without the specific steps yet.

We check from two directions.

  1. From the outside, the way an attacker would: we try the service from outside, just as attackers do. The login screen, the API entrances, the admin screen, files we never meant to make public. We list those entry points, check that each lets in only who it should, and confirm whether a weakness we found can really be reached from outside. Something that is risky in theory and something that can actually be touched from outside are different things.
  2. From the inside, by reading: with your own service, you can see the inside too. The code you wrote, the parts you use (libraries and packages), and your server and cloud settings. We read these three without running them and check for known weaknesses and setting gaps.

Protecting only your own service is not enough. If a partner you connect to, or a system you share with other companies, is broken into, attackers can come in from there; in the October 2026 breaches, one way in was a partner's server. So we also map what your service connects to and which parts and outside services it relies on, and count those risks in the results. That does not mean testing anyone else's site. It means collecting the connections and the known weaknesses in them.

Checking only from outside, or only from inside, leaves gaps. Collect both sets of results in one place, decide what to fix first, and fix it. What you cannot fix yourself, hand to someone who can. That is one full round.

AI tools can chain these checks together without a person giving every instruction. You do not need an expensive AI model or an expert; a cheap model run many times gets you a long way, which is exactly how attackers work too. So even a first-timer can realistically run the whole thing once. From Part 4, I go through it step by step with the promptflow screens.

Checking is also not something you do once. A service keeps changing, and new weaknesses keep being found. If attackers retry automatically, defenders should re-check automatically too. New weaknesses in the parts you use are found almost every day, so the most reliable way is to run the code and library checks automatically every day. Testing from the outside is not a daily job, and it runs against a separate copy, not your live service. The last part of the series shows that setup.

Will testing break my own service?

The natural worry is: "If I use an attack tool on my own service, will it break?" Honestly, depending on how you do it, it can put a load on the service. So Part 3 explains how to test on a separate copy of your setup, or on a copy of the source code, instead of the live service your customers use, and where to draw the line so you do not push too hard. Choose where you test and how hard you push, and there is no need to be afraid. Running your live service without ever checking it is far more dangerous.

Never use these on anyone else's site

One last warning. The tools and ideas in this series are for checking services you own. Never use them on someone else's site, or on any system you do not have the rights to. It breaks the law, and it is the exact opposite of what this series is for. Only check what is yours.

Where the information in this article comes from

What I wrote here about attack tools is based on news reports and public information. The results of testing our own service start in Part 4, with real, unedited screenshots: where we found weaknesses, where we found none, and what was reported as a weakness when it was not.

Next time

Next time, we look inside the tools attackers hold. What does it actually look like, step by step, when an AI runs an attack by itself? As a defender, what should you assume? Again, I will not explain how to get them. The goal is to know what this opponent can do, so you can calmly check your own service.

In this series, in an age when attack tools are free and one click away for anyone, I show step by step how to check your own service yourself and close the gaps before someone else finds them. The target is always our own service; the series does not cover attacking anyone else's site.
If running the checks yourself is hard, EarthLink Network can do the assessment for you. Found a gap you can't fix? We'll handle the fix. Feel free to reach out.
If this was useful, please like and follow.

My point here is not about good or bad. It is a fact: the skill barrier has dropped to almost zero. One short instruction, and anyone, in theory even a child, can move an attack forward. The time when skill itself was the protection is almost over.

Small companies are the least likely to have checked

Small companies are the most exposed to these automated attacks. Large companies have security staff who test their systems regularly, and budget for outside firms. Sole proprietors and companies of a few people have neither. So the businesses that have checked the least are probed by these automated scans just as often as everyone else. They have not checked, so they do not know they have weak spots, and they learn about it only after the leak.

This is why I care about tools that run with one click. If a tool does the planning, a small company without security staff can still run a check at least once. As long as checking takes expert knowledge, people stop at "I know it matters, but we can't." The same thing that lowered the barrier to attack has lowered the barrier to checking. Not all of this is bad news.

Hiding information only hurts the defenders

Whenever I write like this, I get the same pushback: "Don't name those tools. You're giving attackers a lead." I think that idea is backwards.

Attackers do not learn about tools from honest articles like this one. They got them elsewhere, long ago, and that is why they are attacking right now. The pile of breaches in October 2026 is the proof. Keeping quiet did not prevent any of them.

So who is hurt when information is hidden? Only the people with no other way to find it: the defenders. Attackers already know which tools are out there and what they can do; only the defenders do not. They do not even know where they are exposed. That is the most dangerous state to be in.

Defenders benefit from this being public. Once it is known which weakness a tool goes after, software makers can fix it quickly and users can review their settings. If it were hidden, nobody could fix anything, and attackers would quietly keep using it.

It was the same with locks. Keeping a lock's design secret does not help if the lock is weak. A strong lock is strong because it holds even when everyone knows how it works. Software security is the same: do not protect it by hiding, build it to hold up when it is known. That is why, in this series, I name the tools, say what they do, and show the results of checking our own service, without hiding any of it.

First, check your own service yourself

What to do is simple. Take the same tools attackers use, run them against your own service first, find the weak spots, and fix them. If a key that works on almost any lock is on sale, first see whether it works on your own door. If it does, switch to a stronger lock. That is all.

We limit the target to our own service, promptflow, for two reasons. Because it is ours, we decide how far to test, and we can make sure the test copy does not reach real users or outside services. And we are the ones best placed to fix its weak spots. Doing the whole loop of testing, finding, and fixing on something we own seemed the most honest and useful way to show it.

promptflow is a service we build and run for working with AI. Users log in, it holds data, and it connects to other systems through APIs. It has the same kinds of entry points used in the October 2026 breaches, which makes it a good subject. If we find a weak spot in ours, the same spot may be weak in yours. We show the steps exactly as we run them, so you can check the same things on your service.

"Is it safe?" is a call a person makes after testing

I believe that from now on, people's job is to make decisions: AI does the drafting, and people make the final call. "Is my service safe?" is exactly this kind of decision. And a decision needs facts from real testing. Saying "it's probably fine" without testing is not a decision. It is a hope.

Until recently, attackers had the advantage: their attacks were automated, while defenders checked by hand, one thing at a time. Now defenders can use the same automation. If attackers can try with one click, so can we. There is no reason not to use it.

What we will actually do in this series

From Part 4, we test promptflow for real. Here is the approach, without the specific steps yet.

We check from two directions.

  1. From the outside, the way an attacker would: we try the service from outside, just as attackers do. The login screen, the API entrances, the admin screen, files we never meant to make public. We list those entry points, check that each lets in only who it should, and confirm whether a weakness we found can really be reached from outside. Something that is risky in theory and something that can actually be touched from outside are different things.
  2. From the inside, by reading: with your own service, you can see the inside too. The code you wrote, the parts you use (libraries and packages), and your server and cloud settings. We read these three without running them and check for known weaknesses and setting gaps.

Protecting only your own service is not enough. If a partner you connect to, or a system you share with other companies, is broken into, attackers can come in from there; in the October 2026 breaches, one way in was a partner's server. So we also map what your service connects to and which parts and outside services it relies on, and count those risks in the results. That does not mean testing anyone else's site. It means collecting the connections and the known weaknesses in them.

Checking only from outside, or only from inside, leaves gaps. Collect both sets of results in one place, decide what to fix first, and fix it. What you cannot fix yourself, hand to someone who can. That is one full round.

AI tools can chain these checks together without a person giving every instruction. You do not need an expensive AI model or an expert; a cheap model run many times gets you a long way, which is exactly how attackers work too. So even a first-timer can realistically run the whole thing once. From Part 4, I go through it step by step with the promptflow screens.

Checking is also not something you do once. A service keeps changing, and new weaknesses keep being found. If attackers retry automatically, defenders should re-check automatically too. New weaknesses in the parts you use are found almost every day, so the most reliable way is to run the code and library checks automatically every day. Testing from the outside is not a daily job, and it runs against a separate copy, not your live service. The last part of the series shows that setup.

Will testing break my own service?

The natural worry is: "If I use an attack tool on my own service, will it break?" Honestly, depending on how you do it, it can put a load on the service. So Part 3 explains how to test on a separate copy of your setup, or on a copy of the source code, instead of the live service your customers use, and where to draw the line so you do not push too hard. Choose where you test and how hard you push, and there is no need to be afraid. Running your live service without ever checking it is far more dangerous.

Never use these on anyone else's site

One last warning. The tools and ideas in this series are for checking services you own. Never use them on someone else's site, or on any system you do not have the rights to. It breaks the law, and it is the exact opposite of what this series is for. Only check what is yours.

Where the information in this article comes from

What I wrote here about attack tools is based on news reports and public information. The results of testing our own service start in Part 4, with real, unedited screenshots: where we found weaknesses, where we found none, and what was reported as a weakness when it was not.

Next time

Next time, we look inside the tools attackers hold. What does it actually look like, step by step, when an AI runs an attack by itself? As a defender, what should you assume? Again, I will not explain how to get them. The goal is to know what this opponent can do, so you can calmly check your own service.

In this series, in an age when attack tools are free and one click away for anyone, I show step by step how to check your own service yourself and close the gaps before someone else finds them. The target is always our own service; the series does not cover attacking anyone else's site.

title: Composing Any Role from 41 Discrete Permissions: A Gulf Security Review
summary:
A mid-size logistics firm in Dubai runs its warehouse software with a team of six. One person writes code, reviews her own pull requests, and also signs off on production releases, because there is no one else to do it. A bank in Riyadh runs the opposite problem: forty engineers, three of whom are senior enough to be trusted with a production approval, and all three are already booked on other projects when an incident lands at 2am. Neither org fits neatly into 'Developer, QA, Manager, Admin.' Most software doesn't ask them to. It assumes the org chart it was built for.

This is not a theoretical gap. The GCC's tech-talent shortage is acute enough that a large majority of regional organisations report real skills gaps, and the pattern repeats globally — more than half of European firms report they cannot find qualified developers either. When senior engineering time is the scarcest resource in the building, a permission model that forces you to hire around its assumptions is itself a cost.

Why four fixed roles don't survive contact with a real org

A role-based system with four hardcoded roles makes an implicit claim: that 'who can approve a production release' and 'who can view another team's diagnostics' and 'who can see Face Off scores for their department' are all the same question, answerable by the same label. They are not. A QA lead in Abu Dhabi might need to approve staging promotions for two product lines but should never see payroll-adjacent diagnostic output from a third. A founder running a 12-person shop wears the Developer hat on Monday and the Manager hat when a client calls. Fixed roles either over-grant (give the founder QA powers she doesn't need, because the label bundles them) or under-grant (force her to log in under three accounts to get the access her actual job requires).

Corporate AI 365 doesn't ship four roles. It ships 41 discrete permissions and lets an org compose any role it needs from them — including the four consoles (Employee, Developer, QA, Manager) as starting templates, not fixed destinations.

The mechanism: permissions as atoms, roles as compositions

Each permission is a single, auditable capability: submit a plain-language problem report, view a diagnosis and its confidence score, approve a promotion from Developer to QA, approve QA to production, revert a release, connect or disconnect a git provider, view Face Off scores for a given org level, manage another user's permission set. None of these bundle automatically. A role in the system — 'Senior Backend, Payments Team' — is just a named set of permissions attached to a position in the real org hierarchy, which can itself scope what that role sees. Multi-hat is native: one person can hold two roles with two different permission sets, and the system tracks which hat approved which gate.

This matters at the approval gate specifically, because that's where the governance actually lives. Developer → QA → approval → production exists as real git branches and pull requests, and every transition between them is a permission check plus an audit record — who approved, with what confidence score attached to the diagnosis, at what timestamp. A security reviewer's first question is usually 'show me who could have pushed this to production.' With 41 atomic permissions and an org hierarchy behind them, that answer is a query, not a guess.

It's worth being honest about the cost of this design. Forty-one permissions is not a trivial surface. A system this granular can be misconfigured — an admin who grants broadly 'to be safe' recreates the over-grant problem fixed roles were supposed to avoid, just with more knobs. The templates exist precisely to counter that: start from Employee, Developer, QA, or Manager, and subtract or add individual permissions rather than building from zero. The composability is the point; it isn't an invitation to hand every new hire a custom 41-way grant on day one.

What this buys a lean Gulf team specifically

The payoff shows up at the moment that actually costs money. Large-enterprise production downtime runs to a median of roughly US$9,000 a minute by independent industry estimates — a number that makes 'wait for the one senior engineer who understands this module' an expensive default. With permissions composed this precisely, a non-senior developer can be scoped to run diagnosis and raise a fix to QA, while a senior engineer's scarce time is reserved only for the approval gate that genuinely needs judgment. The AI does the root-cause work — file, class, line, a confidence score, a proposed fix, reproducible because it's cached against a hash of the issue and the code snapshot — and a smaller set of trusted people spend their time on the decision, not the detective work.

It also means the person who notices the problem doesn't have to be an engineer at all. Someone in operations or customer service in Doha can file a plain-language report through the Employee console; the permission model decides who sees what happens next, not whether the report gets filed at all. And the trust boundary stays fixed regardless of how permissions are composed: no role, however broadly granted, can reach a live database. The system reasons over source code and a scripted schema export; if a fix genuinely needs live data, it writes a read-only query for your own developer to run, and the result never leaves your environment.

title: Your Docker Image Has 47 Critical CVEs. Here's the 5-Minute Audit That Finds Them.
summary:
Most production Docker images are security debt waiting to be called in. The average enterprise container image carries 200+ known vulnerabilities. About 15% of those are critical or high severity.

Here's a systematic audit process you can run in five minutes.

Step 1: Run Trivy Against Your Image 

docker run --rm -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
  aquasec/trivy image your-image:latest \
  --severity CRITICAL,HIGH \
  --format table

Trivy pulls CVE data from multiple feeds (NVD, GitHub Advisory, Alpine SecDB, etc.) and maps them to your installed packages.

Step 2: Filter by Fixable Vulns Only

The output will include unfixable vulnerabilities — issues in packages where no upstream patch exists yet. Filter those out:

trivy image your-image:latest --ignore-unfixed --severity CRITICAL

Focus your energy where it can make an immediate difference.

Step 3: Trace Back to the Base Image

80% of container CVEs come from the base image, not your application code. If you're on ubuntu:22.04, you're inheriting its entire package surface area. Switch to distroless or minimal variants:

  • gcr.io/distroless/base-debian12 — no shell, no package manager, minimal attack surface
  • alpine:3.19 — if you need a shell, Alpine's minimal footprint dramatically reduces CVE count
  • php:8.2.35-fpm-alpine — application-specific minimal images

Step 4: Pin Exact Versions

FROM php:8.2 resolves to whatever the latest 8.2.x is at build time. After CVE-2026-109618 dropped, images built with a pinned 8.2.34 were vulnerable while teams scrambled to rebuild. Images pinned to 8.2.35 were already protected.

Always pin. Always.

Step 5: Automate in CI

Manual audits are snapshots. Vulnerabilities appear continuously. Add Trivy (or Snyk, Grype) to your CI pipeline so every PR gets a CVE scan before it merges.

The Scale Problem

A single team managing 50+ images cannot run this process manually in any sustainable way. At enterprise scale, the answer isn't better tooling — it's autonomous remediation that identifies the vulnerable image, rebuilds with the patched base, and deploys without waiting for a human to approve each change.

title: AI Found This CVE in 6 Hours. Your Team Would Have Taken 6 Weeks.
summary:
Security research has a discovery problem. Most critical vulnerabilities sit dormant in codebases for months or years before anyone finds them — not because they're hidden, but because manual code review doesn't scale.

The PHP2Shell disclosure changed that calculus.

What the Numbers Actually Mean

When Wiz Research used AI to find CVE-2026-109618 in roughly one week, the real story isn't the CVE — it's the time compression. A team of three senior security researchers, working manually, would typically spend 4–8 weeks to reach the same result. AI didn't replace the researcher. It multiplied their output by 10x.

How the Triage-Pattern-Exploit Loop Works

The methodology Wiz used isn't proprietary magic. It's a reproducible loop:

  1. Ingest the entire codebase — not just the files you think matter, but everything
  2. Apply historical CVE patterns — use prior bugs in the same codebase as fingerprints for similar flaws
  3. Rank by exploitability — not all memory bugs are equal; AI sorts them by proximity to input surfaces
  4. Generate a candidate exploit chain — let the model show the attack path before a human validates it

This loop works because most CVEs in mature codebases share structural DNA with prior CVEs in the same project. PHP's zend engine has had multiple use-after-free bugs. Each one is a training signal.

The Gap This Creates

Organizations that adopt AI-assisted security discovery don't just find bugs faster — they find bugs their competitors haven't found yet. In the current threat environment, that asymmetry is everything.

The attacker community is already using these tools. The question is whether defenders will close that gap or continue relying on annual pen tests and manual code reviews that can't keep up.

What Autonomous Remediation Adds

Discovery is only half the problem. The other half is remediation velocity. When a CVSS 9.2 CVE drops with active exploits in the wild, the organization with autonomous patching deployed wins. The one that kicks off a two-week change management process loses.

Cognitive Daniel is built on exactly this principle — autonomous AI that doesn't just find vulnerabilities but patches them across entire fleets, with zero manual intervention per server.

title: Post-Patch Triage for PHP2Shell: A Practical Checklist for Laravel Servers and Docker
summary:
PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) is fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. This post covers what comes after the update: a triage you can run on a Laravel server, with Docker notes. Commands assume Linux, and paths vary by stack, so adjust them. Everything below is read-only inspection, and none of it replaces a proper forensic process.

Use 2026-10-20 as your cutoff date. That is when the CVE identifiers started circulating, before the patch existed.

1. Confirm the version that serves web traffic

The CLI version is not necessarily the version behind your web server.

php -v
php-fpm -v            # or php-fpm8.2 -v on Debian/Ubuntu
apachectl -M | grep -i php

If you installed from a distribution package, the version string can look old while the fix is present. Check the changelog for the CVE instead:

# Debian/Ubuntu
apt changelog php8.2-fpm | grep -i 'CVE-2026-1096'
# RHEL family
rpm -q --changelog php-fpm | grep -i 'CVE-2026-1096'

Updating Laravel does not update PHP. Restart PHP-FPM, Apache and any long-running workers (queue workers, Octane) after the update.

2. Docker

Each container carries its own PHP. The host's PHP does not matter here.

docker exec  php -v
docker build --pull --no-cache -t myapp:2026-10-22 .
docker compose pull && docker compose up -d --build

Watch for tags pinned to an old patch version (for example php:8.2.30-fpm). --pull will not move those. Edit the tag. Rebuild queue worker and scheduler containers too, not only the web one.

3. Files that should not be there 

# PHP files modified since the cutoff, excluding dependency folders
find /var/www -type f -name '*.php' -newermt '2026-10-20' \
  -not -path '*/vendor/*' -not -path '*/node_modules/*'

# PHP-like files where none should live
find /var/www/app/storage /var/www/app/public/uploads -type f \
  \( -name '*.php' -o -name '*.phtml' -o -name '*.phar' \)

# If the deploy directory is a git checkout
git -C /var/www/app status --porcelain

Legitimate deploys also change files, so compare against your deploy history before panicking.

4. Persistence 

sudo ls -la /etc/cron.d /var/spool/cron/crontabs 2>/dev/null
systemctl list-timers --all
awk -F: '$3 >= 1000 {print $1}' /etc/passwd
sudo find /home /root -name authorized_keys -exec ls -l {} +
last -n 20

You are looking for anything you cannot explain: a job, a timer, a user or a key nobody on your team added.

5. Logs

The researchers suggest watching for unusual multipart requests followed by memory limit errors, repeated HTTP 500 responses, oversized PHPSESSID response cookies and unexplained worker restarts.

grep -i 'allowed memory size' /var/log/php*-fpm.log | tail -50
awk '$9 == 500 {print $1}' /var/log/nginx/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

The status field position assumes the common log format. Adjust if yours differs.

6. Rotate what a worker could have held

The flaws can expose worker memory, so assume anything the app handles could have been read. At minimum:

  • database passwords
  • third-party API keys and mail credentials
  • APP_KEY, with care: rotating it invalidates sessions and anything encrypted with it. Recent Laravel versions support APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS for graceful rotation, so check the docs for your version.
  • active sessions (clear the session table or files)

Then run php artisan config:clear and redeploy.

7. Where a scanner fits

A filesystem scanner is one useful input here. Laravel Scalpel (open source, my project) covers a defined slice: PHP and PHP-like extensions in non-PHP zones such as public and storage, common obfuscation patterns, dangerous .htaccess and .user.ini directives, .env integrity, and a baseline diff.   • Trigger it from outside the app's user. An in-app run uses the same OS user as PHP, so an attacker with code execution could tamper with it.   • A WAF rule is a stopgap. Cloudflare itself said attackers adapted payloads around its rules.

title: How Wiz Found PHP2Shell With AI in One Week — and How AI Now Fixes It at Enterprise Scale
summary:
Today Wiz Research disclosed PHP2Shell — two critical memory-safety bugs in PHP's core engine that allow unauthenticated remote code execution on 70% of the internet. CVSS 9.2. Active exploits in the wild. 22.6 million vulnerable servers identified in the first hours after disclosure.

What most writeups will miss: the story of how Wiz found it is more important than the CVE itself.

How Wiz Actually Found This

Wiz didn't stumble onto PHP2Shell. They went hunting using Wiz Atlas, augmented with Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol.

Step 1 — Triage at scale: Wiz Atlas ingested PHP's entire C source tree and flagged 47 highest-risk functions. One researcher triaged in hours what previously took a team weeks.

Step 2 — Bug pattern matching: Gemini 4 Argon applied patterns from prior PHP CVEs to identify zend_exception_handle() as a use-after-free candidate.

Step 3 — Exploit chain construction: GPT-5.6 Sol generated a working exploit chain. Human researcher validated. Total time: ~one week.

Step 4 — Patch validation: Automated regression testing confirmed PHP 8.2.35 as the fix. One researcher. One week. CVSS 9.2.

What PHP2Shell Does

CVE-2026-109618: Use-after-free in zend_exception_handle() during fatal error cleanup triggered by crafted multipart/form-data POST. No auth required.

CVE-2026-109619: Same class of bug in OPcache during memory constraint checks.

Patch Table

PHP Branch Vulnerable Patched Notes
8.4.x ≤ 8.4.26 8.4.27
8.3.x ≤ 8.3.35 8.3.36
8.2.x ≤ 8.2.34 8.2.35
8.1.x All versions ❌ No upstream patch Branch upgrade required

The Fix (3 files, no logic changes)

Dockerfile:

FROM php:8.2.35-fpm-alpine  # was 8.2.34

composer.json:

"platform": { "php": "8.2.35" }

CI pipeline:

php-version: '8.2.35'  # was '8.2.34'

The Bigger Picture: AI-Assisted Discovery Changes Everything

This is not just a story about a PHP bug. It's a signal that AI-augmented security research has arrived at production scale. What Wiz demonstrated with Gemini and GPT-5.6 Sol is the same capability being built into autonomous engineering platforms.

At Cognitive Daniel, we're applying this same principle in reverse — not just finding vulnerabilities, but autonomously patching them across entire enterprise fleets. The same AI-accelerated pattern recognition that Wiz used to discover CVE-2026-109618 in a week can be used to remediate it across thousands of servers without human intervention per-server.

Proof-of-concept: https://github.com/2badagoldman/cognitive-daniel/tree/main/demos/php2shell-fix

Full writeup: https://www.cognitivedaniel.com/blog/wiz-found-php2shell-daniel-fixes-it-at-scale

*If your team is still patching PHP vulnerabilities manually server-by-server, [let's talk] https://www.cognitivedaniel.com/
